blocks.text: There follows in the Prophet: Taking them up, it carries them on its wings. Literally, it takes him up, it carries him. But him means any one of them. Or him means them, by an enallage of number. Or it refers to the more remote noun, that is, to nest, a word which we have said means the brood. Upon its feathers, or upon its wings. In Hebrew, על אברתו. The Greeks: ἐπὶ τῶν μεταφρένων αὐτοῦ [epi tōn metaphrenōn autou]. Hence Jerome: on its shoulders. For the eagle is thought to carry not only with its beak or talons, but also with its shoulders and wings. Thus in Plutarch, On Civil Instruction: Αἰσώπου βασίλισκος ἐπὶ τῶν ὤμων τοῦ ἀετοῦ κομισθεὶς [Aisōpou basiliskos epi tōn ōmōn tou aetou komistheis], Aesop's wren, carried on the shoulders of the eagle, etc. In Aelian, Hist. book 12, ch. 21, when Tilgamus, a Babylonian boy, was falling headlong from the top of the citadel, ὁ αἰετὸς, πρὶν ἢ τῇ γῇ προσαῤῥαχθῆναι τὸ βρέφος, ὑπῆλθεν αὐτὸ, καὶ τὰ νῶτα ὑπέβαλεν [ho aietos, prin ē tē gē prosarrhachthēnai to brephos, hypēlthen auto, kai ta nōta hypebalen] (or κατὰ νῶτα ὑπέλαβεν [kata nōta hypelaben], as it reads in Apostolius, Proverb 1793), before he was dashed against the ground, the eagle came beneath him and caught him on its back. Aristomenes too, in Pausanias' Messeniaca, when he had been thrown by the Lacedaemonians into the Caeadas: ὄρνιθα τὸν ἀετὸν ὑποπέτεσθαί (φασι) καὶ ἀνέχειν ταῖς πτέρυξιν, ἐς ὃ κατήνεγκεν αὐτὸν ἐς τὸ πέρας, οὔτε πηρωθέντα οὐδὲν τοῦ σώματος, οὔτε τραῦμα ἐπιλαβόντα [ornitha ton aeton hypopetesthai (phasi) kai anechein tais pteryxin, es ho katēnenken auton es to peras, oute pērōthenta ouden tou sōmatos, oute trauma epilabonta], they say that an eagle flew beneath him and held him up with its wings until it had brought him down to the bottom neither maimed nor injured in any part. I do not offer these as true, but as fables invented by people who were convinced that it is not foreign to the eagle's nature to carry something on its shoulders and wings in flight itself. Yet I by no means think that the chicks are carried by eagles in continuous transport. It is only likely that those eager to fly, and failing in the very attempt, are caught and held up by their parents' wings until, having regained courage, they dare to commit themselves to the air again. R. Selomo offers something else, more subtle than solid: כשבא ליטלן ממקום למקום אינו נוטלן ברגליו כשאר עופות לפי ששאר עופות יראים מן הנשר שהוא מגביה לעוף ופורח עליהם לפיכך נושאין ברגליו מפני הנשר אבל הנשר אינו ירא אלא מן החץ לפיכך נושאן על כנפיו אומר מוטב שיכנס החץ בי ולא יכנס בבני, When the eagle moves its chicks from place to place, it does not carry them in its feet as other birds do, because these fear the eagle, which soars aloft in flight and flies higher than they; and therefore they carry [II, 763] their chicks in their feet, so as not to expose them to the eagle. But the eagle fears nothing except the arrow; that is why it carries its chicks on its wings, as if saying to itself: Better that the arrow strike me than my chicks. But this invention does not please me, because neither does the eagle on its back, nor do other birds in their feet, usually move their chicks from place to place by deliberate design. And if they did, they would do it by the sole guidance of nature, not for the reasons alleged, about which no one will persuade me that birds reflect. In Isidore, Orig. book 12, ch. 7: The tuci (as he calls cuckoos with an old Spanish word) have a set time of coming, carried on the shoulders of kites because of their short and small flights, lest, exhausted over long stretches of air, they should fail. If this were reported by a reliable writer, it would shed no little light on what has been said about the eagle carrying its chicks. [col. 180] But apart from Isidore, a writer hardly skilled in natural history, none of the older authors is found asserting the same. Yet, if we believe Aelian, Hist. book 7, ch. 17, their mates the ceryli, worn out by old age, αἱ ἀλκυόνες περιάγουσιν ἐπ᾽ αὐτῶν τῶν καλουμένων μετοπτερυγίων [hai alkyones periagousin ep᾽ autōn tōn kaloumenōn metopterygiōn], the halcyons carry about upon what are called the interscapulars. Hence Plutarch on the halcyon in the book Whether Land or Sea Animals: Ὅταν δὲ διὰ γῆρας ἀσθενὴς ὁ ἄῤῥην γένηται, συνέπεσθαι καὶ βαρὺς, ὑπολαβοῦσα γηροφορεῖ, καὶ γηροτροφεῖ [Hotan de dia gēras asthenēs ho arrhēn genētai, synepesthai kai barys, hypolabousa gērophorei, kai gērotrophei]; taking up the male, now heavy with years and following with difficulty, she carries and feeds him. And long before, Antigonus had taught the same, Hist. 27: Τῶν δὲ ἀλκυόνων οἱ ἄρσενες κήρυλοι καλοῦνται. ὅτ᾽ ἂν οὖν ὑπὸ τοῦ γήρως ἀσθενήσωσι, καὶ μηκέτι δύνωνται πέτεσθαι, φέρουσιν αὐτοὺς αἱ θήλειαι, ἐπὶ τῶν πτερῶν λαβοῦσαι [Tōn de alkyonōn hoi arsenes kēryloi kalountai. hot᾽ an oun hypo tou gērōs asthenēsōsi, kai mēketi dynōntai petesthai, pherousin autous hai thēleiai, epi tōn pterōn labousai]; The males of the halcyons are called ceryli. When they are weak from old age and can no longer fly, the females take them up on their wings and carry them. Hence that well-known saying of Alcman, quoted in the same place: Οὔ μ᾽ ἔτι παρθενικαὶ [Ou m᾽ eti parthenikai], etc. The same is also told of storks. The Scholiast on Aristophanes, on the Birds: Οἱ γὰρ πελαργοὶ, δικαιοπραγεῖς ὄντες, ἐπὶ πτερῶν βαδίζουσι τοὺς πατέρας γεγηρακότας βαστάζοντες [Hoi gar pelargoi, dikaiopragеis ontes, epi pterōn badizousi tous pateras gegērakotas bastazontes]; Storks, since they observe justice, migrate carrying on their wings their fathers, worn out with age. So also Suidas under Ἀντιπελαργεῖν [Antipelargein]. And Basil, Hexaemeron, Homily 8: Τὴν δυνατὴν καὶ ἐν τῇ πτήσει παρέχονται βοήθειαν, ἠρέμα τῷ πτερῷ κουφίζοντες ἑκατέρωθεν [Tēn dynatēn kai en tē ptēsei parechontai boētheian, ērema tō pterō kouphizontes hekaterōthen]. And Eustathius of Antioch: Εἰ δὲ τῇ πτήσει ὑποκάτωθεν αὐτὸν ὑποβαστάζουσιν, καὶ τοῖς ἰδίοις πτεροῖς ἠρέμα αὐτὸν ὑποκουφίζουσιν ἑκατέρωθεν [Ei de tē ptēsei hypokatōthen auton hypobastazousin, kai tois idiois pterois ērema auton hypokouphizousin hekaterōthen]. From the same source Ambrose, Hexaemeron book 5, ch. 16: so that, lifting up the old one from this side and that with the prop of their wings, they exercise him in flying. Tacitus also tells the fable that the phoenix takes up its father's body. That is why Artemidorus declares that whoever sees a phoenix in his dreams will be reduced to such poverty that he will be forced, after the manner of the phoenix, to carry out his parent's corpse on his own shoulders. See the distinguished Vossius on Mela, p. 297.
